ArtifactCollection.description: What one collection pass reclaimed, or would reclaim in a dry run.
ArtifactCollection.title: ArtifactCollection

ArtifactHold.description:
An explicit claim that keeps one artifact out of any future collection.

References answer "is something still going to run this". A hold answers a
question references cannot: "a human still needs this" -- a callable under
investigation, a result cited outside Eyvan, a workspace pinned for a repro.
Without it the only way to protect such an object is to keep a workload alive
around it, which spends capacity to express a bookkeeping fact.

One hold per artifact, deliberately. A hold *set* would need its own identity,
ownership and expiry semantics, and the failure it prevents -- two people each
believing the other's hold protects the object -- is not one this package has
seen. The single hold names its owner and reason, so a second person finds a
stated claim to argue with rather than an anonymous flag.
ArtifactHold.title: ArtifactHold

ArtifactHoldRequest.description: Place an explicit human claim on one scoped indexed artifact.
ArtifactHoldRequest.title: ArtifactHoldRequest

ArtifactInventoryEntry.description: One non-destructive comparison at an explicit tenant-scoped URI.
ArtifactInventoryEntry.title: ArtifactInventoryEntry

ArtifactInventoryReindexRequest.description: Explicit additive repair for one previously inspected scope page.
ArtifactInventoryReindexRequest.title: ArtifactInventoryReindexRequest

ArtifactInventoryStatus.description: Relationship between one scoped index row and one physical object.
ArtifactInventoryStatus.title: ArtifactInventoryStatus

ArtifactReferenceRecord.description:
One workload's claim on one artifact: the reverse index.

Nothing could previously answer "which workloads use this callable?", so
"unreferenced" was not a computable property and no collector could be
written safely. A reference is created when a workload that names an
artifact is stored, and released when that workload reaches a terminal
state -- but the row is *kept*, because the history of who referenced what is
what makes a later deletion auditable.
ArtifactReferenceRecord.title: ArtifactReferenceRecord

ArtifactUsage.description: Indexed artifact bytes in one scope, and the ceiling they are measured against.
ArtifactUsage.title: ArtifactUsage

AttachmentRequest.description: Closed, credential-free inputs accepted by the attachment CLI.
AttachmentRequest.title: AttachmentRequest

AuditEvent.description: Immutable, ordered audit event emitted by a committed transaction.
AuditEvent.title: AuditEvent

AutoscaleBlockReason.description: Durable reason an autoscaler cannot add a workload's required capacity.
AutoscaleBlockReason.title: AutoscaleBlockReason

AvailabilityPolicy.description:
How hard a pool backs off, and how fast it forgets.

These were constants, and the wrong ones for somebody. How long to wait
after a zone says no is a property of *that* zone and that purchase class:
a spot TPU pool in a contended region is worth asking again in a minute,
while a pool whose provider is rate-limiting the account is not. A single
curve compiled into the planner meant an operator watching the wrong
behaviour had no way to say so, and the only lever left was to delete the
pool.

Defaults reproduce the constants exactly, so a fleet that declares nothing
behaves as it always did.
AvailabilityPolicy.title: AvailabilityPolicy

BatchSubmitRequest.description: Fan out one template into ``count`` ordinary durable workloads.
BatchSubmitRequest.title: BatchSubmitRequest

BatchSubmitResponse.description: The coordinator plus its tasks, in task order.
BatchSubmitResponse.title: BatchSubmitResponse

BudgetGrantIssueRequest.description:
Cut a slice of one tenant's budget for one peer plane.

``expires_at`` is required and has no default. A grant that cannot lapse
turns a home plane going away permanently into unbounded spend on every peer
that ever held one, so the record refuses to be built without it -- and a
default here would be this layer quietly choosing how long that risk lasts.
BudgetGrantIssueRequest.title: BudgetGrantIssueRequest

BudgetGrantRecord.description:
One slice of a tenant's budget, issued by its home plane to a peer.

The grant is the peer's *entire* authority to spend for this tenant. It has an
expiry with no default of "never", because a grant that cannot lapse turns a
home plane that goes away permanently into an unbounded spend on every peer
that ever held one.
BudgetGrantRecord.title: BudgetGrantRecord

BudgetRecord.description: Monetary admission budget for an organization project.
BudgetRecord.title: BudgetRecord

BudgetStatus.description:
A budget's spend, its period window, and where it is heading.

Two of these fields revive dashboard surfaces that could never populate:
``forecast`` was typed and never set, so "Current forecast" always read
Unavailable and the alert block behind it could not fire; ``period_ends_at``
is what makes ``spent`` interpretable at all, since a number with no window
attached cannot be compared to a limit that has one.
BudgetStatus.title: BudgetStatus

BuildResponse.description:
What code this control plane is made of.

Every component of this system reports one version string, so a caller
cannot tell from it whether the plane it is talking to is the build a
receipt was minted against. ``source_digest`` distinguishes them; it is
``None``, with ``digest_detail`` saying why, when it could not be computed
in full -- never a digest over the part of the tree that happened to be
readable.
BuildResponse.title: BuildResponse

CallableExecution.description: Reference to a callable artifact in trusted object storage.
CallableExecution.title: CallableExecution

CandidateZone.description:
One pool this workload accepts, and what is known about it.

The belief state -- cooldowns and consecutive provider failures -- has
decided which pool a cross-zone workload asks next since alternates
existed, and said so nowhere. "Why is it waiting on us-east5-b when
us-central2-b is idle" had no answer short of reading cell records by hand,
and on a spot-first fleet it is the question asked most often.

Attributes:
    pool_id: The pool, which for a cross-zone shape is effectively the zone.
    zone: Where it is, when the pool records one.
    preferred: Whether this is the pool the planner would ask next.
    free_owned_cells: Cells this workload already owns here, which it could
        take immediately. The strongest reason to prefer a pool.
    free_shared_cells: Unreserved cells of the right width here.
    cooling_cells: Cells in a provider-failure cooldown. A pool is as cold
        as its coldest cell, which is why one is enough to rank it lower.
    consecutive_failures: The worst consecutive-failure count here.
CandidateZone.title: CandidateZone

CapacityBeliefState.description: Persisted empirical availability evidence for one execution cell.
CapacityBeliefState.title: CapacityBeliefState

CapacityClass.description: Canonical capacity purchase classes used at the API boundary.
CapacityClass.title: CapacityClass

CapacityPoolRecord.description: Declarative node type used by the capacity autoscaler.
CapacityPoolRecord.title: CapacityPoolRecord

CapacityPoolResponse.description: One available pool advertised by the control plane.
CapacityPoolResponse.title: CapacityPoolResponse

CapacityProviderFailureCode.description: Stable machine-readable reason for a capacity-provider failure.
CapacityProviderFailureCode.title: CapacityProviderFailureCode

CapacityResponse.description: Advertised capacity inventory across all applied fleets.
CapacityResponse.title: CapacityResponse

CapacityRetryProgress.description: Durable state of the newest relevant capacity-apply command.
CapacityRetryProgress.title: CapacityRetryProgress

CapacityStatus.description:
Provider-neutral lifecycle state for one capacity cell.

Provider adapters map their raw cloud states into this closed set before
observations reach drivers, persistence, the agent wire, or the control
plane. ``REQUESTING`` is the sole control-plane-owned state: it records
that Eyvan is about to issue a provider request, not that a provider has
begun provisioning capacity.
CapacityStatus.title: CapacityStatus

CarbonReport.description:
Grid intensity across the regions the fleet actually occupies.

Deliberately not part of placement. A carbon number that silently steered
scheduling would produce decisions that look deliberate and are not, so this
is a report and only a report until someone brings a source they trust; a
test asserts the placement path does not import the module behind it.
CarbonReport.title: CarbonReport

CellBillingReport.description: Accrued and idle cell cost over a fleet or one pool.
CellBillingReport.title: CellBillingReport

CellRejection.description: One cell-specific reason a workload could not be placed there.
CellRejection.title: CellRejection

CellState.description: Observed availability of an execution cell.
CellState.title: CellState

CommandExecution.description: A shell command submitted to a cell execution backend.
CommandExecution.title: CommandExecution

CoordinationKind.description:
What a coordinator record coordinates, and therefore how it settles.

A coordinator owns children and has no lease of its own, so nothing but a
dedicated controller phase can ever settle it. Naming the kind explicitly --
rather than inferring "coordinator" from ``schedulable is False`` -- keeps that
phase from capturing unrelated unschedulable records as they are introduced.
CoordinationKind.title: CoordinationKind

CredentialRotationRecord.description:
One rotation of one signing credential, and how it ended.

Durable in a table of its own, and additive for the same reason
:class:`WorkloadAttemptTopology` is: a field on an existing persisted record
would be decoded with ``extra='forbid'`` by a rolled-back replica, and the
first rotation would make that record unreadable. A replica that predates
this table never selects from it and simply does not rotate.

**No material, and nothing derived from material.** Not the new key, not the
old one, and deliberately not a digest either: a digest of a credential is an
offline cracking target that an audit reader, a backup, and a support bundle
would all carry. A generation number is enough to say which material is in
effect, and it is the only thing here that refers to it.

The row is what lets two replicas agree, so ``previous_not_after`` is the
definite point at which the superseded generation stops verifying **fleet
wide** rather than per process.
CredentialRotationRecord.title: CredentialRotationRecord

CredentialRotationState.description: How one rotation of one credential ended, or that it has not ended.
CredentialRotationState.title: CredentialRotationState

DagNodeRequest.description: One named stage and the sibling stages it waits for.
DagNodeRequest.title: DagNodeRequest

DagSubmitRequest.description: Submit a small pipeline of dependent workloads in one transaction.
DagSubmitRequest.title: DagSubmitRequest

DagSubmitResponse.description: The coordinator plus its nodes, in topological order.
DagSubmitResponse.title: DagSubmitResponse

EffectiveProjectScope.description:
One project the authenticated principal can act in.

``permissions`` is evaluated by the same :class:`Authorizer` used at every
service boundary after claim and durable grants have been unioned. It is not
a client-side interpretation of an access-token payload.
EffectiveProjectScope.title: EffectiveProjectScope

EffectiveQuota.description:
Every quota that applies to one scope, and whether any of them bind.

Admission walks the whole chain and enforces *every* quota it finds, so
"the quota that applies" is not one row. Reporting the narrowest stored row
would answer a question nobody asked, and reporting a 404 when nothing is
stored -- which is what this used to do -- calls the ordinary state of a
fresh fleet an error.

``unlimited`` is the honest reading of an empty hierarchy: no scope declares
a limit, so nothing here constrains the workload. It is stated rather than
left to be inferred from an empty list, because an empty list is exactly
what a caller would also see if the read had silently failed.
EffectiveQuota.title: EffectiveQuota

FleetInitScriptRequest.description: A fleet's bash init script; an empty string removes it.
FleetInitScriptRequest.title: FleetInitScriptRequest

FleetStatusResponse.description: Server-side pool and cell state for one applied fleet.
FleetStatusResponse.title: FleetStatusResponse

GcpQueueAdmissionDenialTarget.description: Exact GCP TPU target rejected before it entered the capacity queue.
GcpQueueAdmissionDenialTarget.title: GcpQueueAdmissionDenialTarget

GrantState.description: Lifecycle of one budget or quota grant.
GrantState.title: GrantState

GroupRoleRequest.description: One named shape within a group, and how many of it the group needs.
GroupRoleRequest.title: GroupRoleRequest

GroupSubmitRequest.description: Submit differently-shaped workloads that must admit together.
GroupSubmitRequest.title: GroupSubmitRequest

GroupSubmitResponse.description: The coordinator plus its gated members.
GroupSubmitResponse.title: GroupSubmitResponse

LaunchLatencyReport.description: Provisioning latency across every pool, at one moment.
LaunchLatencyReport.title: LaunchLatencyReport

LeaseRecord.description: Fenced assignment of one workload to one execution cell.
LeaseRecord.title: LeaseRecord

LeaseState.description: Fenced ownership states for capacity leases.
LeaseState.title: LeaseState

ManagedArtifactRecord.description:
Fenced ledger entry for one tenant-scoped physical object.

``record_generation`` fences stale database actors while ``object_version``
fences provider mutations.  Rows are retained as zero-byte tombstones after
deletion; a later upload advances the generation instead of resurrecting an
old claim in place.

quarantine_reason.default: legacy object version has not been verified
quarantine_reason.title: Quarantine Reason

ManagedArtifactRecord.title: ManagedArtifactRecord

ManagedArtifactState.description: Durable lifecycle of one scoped managed object.
ManagedArtifactState.title: ManagedArtifactState

NativeContainerConfig.description:
Structured OCI execution settings for an Eyvan-native workload.

This intentionally exposes only stable runtime properties. Arbitrary Docker
command-line flags are not part of Eyvan's durable fleet API.
NativeContainerConfig.title: NativeContainerConfig

NativeContainerMount.description: One explicit host path made available to an Eyvan-native OCI workload.
NativeContainerMount.title: NativeContainerMount

NativeRuntimeArtifact.description: A GCS artifact staged on every native capacity host before work starts.
NativeRuntimeArtifact.title: NativeRuntimeArtifact

NativeRuntimeConfig.description:
Declarative host setup and workload defaults for Eyvan-native cells.

The configuration is deliberately host-oriented. ``vm_image`` selects a
GCP Compute OS image, while ``container`` describes OCI execution handled
by the Eyvan-native runtime.
NativeRuntimeConfig.title: NativeRuntimeConfig

NoMatchingCapacityPoolErrorContext.description: Fleet inventory returned when callable placement has no exact pool.
NoMatchingCapacityPoolErrorContext.title: NoMatchingCapacityPoolErrorContext

NoMatchingCapacityPoolErrorResponse.description: Structured API response for an unavailable accelerator in one fleet.
NoMatchingCapacityPoolErrorResponse.title: NoMatchingCapacityPoolErrorResponse

OrganizationRecord.description:
A tenant this control plane knows about.

Until this existed, ``org_id`` was a free-form string on every request and a
tenant was whatever anyone typed. Nothing could answer "which organizations
exist", so nothing could list them, bill them, or refuse a typo -- a
``PUT /quotas`` naming ``acmee`` created a quota for a tenant that would
never submit anything, and it looked exactly like success.

Registration is deliberately thin. It is a name and an owner, not a
settings object: quotas, budgets and policies are already their own records
scoped by ``org_id``, and duplicating any of them here would create two
places to look and one of them wrong.
OrganizationRecord.title: OrganizationRecord

OrganizationRegisterRequest.description:
Register or update one tenant.

``id`` comes from the path, so it is absent here: two spellings of the same
identity in one request is a mismatch waiting to be resolved silently in
whichever direction the handler happens to prefer.
OrganizationRegisterRequest.title: OrganizationRegisterRequest

OutboxState.description: Delivery state for a transactional backend command.
OutboxState.title: OutboxState

Permission.description: Actions enforced by the service authorization policy.
Permission.title: Permission

PlacementMode.description:
How a workload's workers may be distributed over capacity cells.

ATOMIC is the exact-shape contract: one cell whose worker count equals the
workload's, one provider resource, one hardware world. ELASTIC is the
node-pool contract: workers are packed from any combination of cells of the
right accelerator type -- warm cells first, provisioning only the deficit --
and the workload runs as one lease group with one hardware world per cell.

ELASTIC requires ``WorkerResourceScope.PER_WORKER``; a legacy gang that
encodes a whole atomic cell has no per-worker shape to pack from.
PlacementMode.title: PlacementMode

PlanePeerPutRequest.description:
Register another control plane this one may grant budget to.

``plane_id`` comes from the path for the same reason it does on an
organization: one identity, spelled once.
PlanePeerPutRequest.title: PlanePeerPutRequest

PlanePeerRecord.description:
Another control plane this one knows about.

Deliberately not a cluster membership protocol. A peer is a URL an operator
wrote down, because the alternative -- planes discovering each other -- means
a joining plane can claim a tenant's budget by asserting it is the home, and
there is no authority in this design that could refuse.
PlanePeerRecord.title: PlanePeerRecord

PolicyRecord.description: Placement policy for an organization project.
PolicyRecord.title: PolicyRecord

PoolCallableSubmitRequest.description: Callable intent whose TPU placement is derived from an enabled Spot fleet pool.
PoolCallableSubmitRequest.title: PoolCallableSubmitRequest

PoolEstimate.description: What one pool would charge for one workload, and where the price came from.
PoolEstimate.title: PoolEstimate

PoolLaunchLatency.description:
How long one pool takes to hand over usable capacity, and on what evidence.

The scheduler has ranked pools by this number since it existed -- ``p95`` of
the same ``provision_latencies_s`` samples -- and nothing ever showed it to
the person deciding which pool to ask for. "Why did my job land in the slow
region" had no answer that did not involve reading the scheduler.

``samples`` is reported beside every percentile and is not decoration. A p95
over three provisions is not a p95, and a report that presented one as
equivalent to a p95 over three hundred would be inviting exactly the
confident wrong decision this exists to prevent.
PoolLaunchLatency.title: PoolLaunchLatency

PoolWarmth.description:
Whether one pool's warm floor is currently held, and what it costs.

A warm window is a promise an operator wrote and nothing reported on. Two
things go wrong invisibly: the floor is not met, so the 09:00 latency the
window exists to prevent happens anyway; or the floor is met and the cells sit
unused, which is *correct* and looks identical to waste in every other view.

That second case is why this joins the billing clock. Warm capacity is
deliberately idle. Without a way to name it, an operator reading idle cost
cannot tell the capacity they asked to keep hot from the capacity their
packing is wasting, and the only safe reaction to an unexplained idle number
is to delete the warm floor -- undoing the fix.
PoolWarmth.title: PoolWarmth

PoolWorkloadSubmitRequest.description: Command intent whose infrastructure contract is derived from a fleet node type.
PoolWorkloadSubmitRequest.title: PoolWorkloadSubmitRequest

ProjectRecord.description:
A project inside one registered organization.

Scoped by ``(org_id, id)`` because project names are only unique within a
tenant: two organizations both having a ``research`` project is the ordinary
case, and a globally unique project id would make the second one impossible
to create for reasons no user could see.
ProjectRecord.title: ProjectRecord

ProjectRegisterRequest.description: Register or update one project inside a registered organization.
ProjectRegisterRequest.title: ProjectRegisterRequest

ProjectUsageReport.description: Per-subject usage across one project, newest activity first.
ProjectUsageReport.title: ProjectUsageReport

QueueTrend.description:
Queue pressure over recent time, derived from the audit ledger.

Bucketed by wall clock, not by event count: the question is "is the queue
growing", and count-based buckets compress exactly the quiet periods that
answer it.
QueueTrend.title: QueueTrend

QueueTrendPoint.description: One time bucket of the submitted-vs-admitted trend.
QueueTrendPoint.title: QueueTrendPoint

QuotaGrantIssueRequest.description:
Cut a slice of one tenant's quota for one peer plane.

``limits`` is a resource vector rather than a scalar, and omitted dimensions
are zero. A slice that silently authorized every resource it forgot to
mention would be the opposite of a ceiling.
QuotaGrantIssueRequest.title: QuotaGrantIssueRequest

QuotaGrantRecord.description:
One slice of a tenant's *quota*, issued by its home plane to a peer.

The same hole as budgets, in a different currency. ``QuotaRecord.limits`` is
one durable vector in one database, so a tenant with projects on three planes
could run three times its TPU ceiling with every plane locally compliant.
Money and chips are separate limits and a fleet can hold one while breaching
the other -- a tenant granted a small budget on cheap Spot capacity can still
exhaust an accelerator pool everyone else is queued for.

Deliberately a mirror of :class:`BudgetGrantRecord` rather than a
generalization of it. The two differ in exactly one place -- a scalar becomes
a vector, and headroom therefore has to hold in *every* dimension at once --
and collapsing them into one generic grant would put that difference behind a
type parameter where nobody reviewing an admission decision would see it.
QuotaGrantRecord.title: QuotaGrantRecord

QuotaRecord.description: Hierarchical resource quota and DRF weight.
QuotaRecord.title: QuotaRecord

ReadOnlyQueryRequest.description: One ad-hoc read against this plane's own database.
ReadOnlyQueryRequest.title: ReadOnlyQueryRequest

ReadOnlyQueryResponse.description:
Rows, and whether there were more of them.

``truncated`` is reported rather than left to the caller to infer from the
row count against the limit: those are indistinguishable when a result
exactly fills the cap, and reading a cut-short answer as a complete one is
the mistake this surface must not make easy.
ReadOnlyQueryResponse.title: ReadOnlyQueryResponse

RegionCarbon.description:
What is known about one region's grid intensity, including nothing.

``intensity`` is null and ``reason`` is populated whenever there is no
usable reading, which today is always: no provider ships. Reported rather
than omitted, because an operator asking about carbon deserves the answer
"nothing is configured" instead of an empty list they have to interpret.
RegionCarbon.title: RegionCarbon

ResearchBudget.description: What a research plan may spend; enforced by the plane, never by the model.
ResearchBudget.title: ResearchBudget

ResourceGang.description: Atomic group of equal resource bundles.
ResourceGang.title: ResourceGang

ResourceHours.description: Fractional resource-time quantities used only for accounting.
ResourceHours.title: ResourceHours

ResourceLimits.description: Resource limit vector whose omitted scalar dimensions mean zero.
ResourceLimits.title: ResourceLimits

ResourceVector.description: Scalar resources requested by one workload replica or offered by a cell.
ResourceVector.title: ResourceVector

Role.description: Organization and project roles understood by the control plane.
Role.title: Role

RoleGrant.description: A role scoped to a fleet, organization, or project.
RoleGrant.title: RoleGrant

RoleGrantIssueRequest.description:
Grant one role to one subject, durably.

The grant's scope travels inside ``grant`` rather than as sibling fields, so
``RoleGrant``'s own validation -- fleet admin is unscoped, project roles
require a project -- applies here instead of being restated and drifting.
RoleGrantIssueRequest.title: RoleGrantIssueRequest

RoleGrantRecord.description:
A durable role grant this control plane issued and can revoke.

Until this existed, ``eyvan_grants`` in an OIDC token was the *only* source
of authority, so onboarding a tenant meant configuring an identity provider
to mint a bespoke claim that deserializes into ``tuple[RoleGrant, ...]`` --
a claim mentioned nowhere in the README. Anyone whose IdP could not be
taught a custom claim could not use Eyvan's authorization at all, and
revoking access meant an IdP change rather than an API call.

The claim is still honored. This is a second source, not a replacement:
a deployment that already mints the claim keeps working, and one that cannot
now has somewhere to put grants. They are unioned, because a grant from
either source is a grant the operator made.

Keyed by ``(subject, role, org_id, project_id)`` so re-issuing the same
grant overwrites rather than accumulating -- there is no meaningful
difference between holding one copy of a role and holding two.
RoleGrantRecord.title: RoleGrantRecord

RulesBody.description:
One account's governance rules: ``null`` clears a rule, an omitted key keeps the stored value.

Omission is preserved so a client written before a rule existed (which never
sends its key) cannot clear it by accident. The dashboard sends only edits;
``eyvan users rules`` sends every key, so its omitted options still clear.
RulesBody.title: RulesBody

ScopeQuota.description:
One scope of the quota hierarchy, and whether anything is declared there.

Attributes:
    scope: ``org``, ``project`` or ``principal``.
    org_id / project_id / principal_id: the scope's identity.
    quota: the record declared at this scope, or ``None`` when nothing is.
        Absence means this scope imposes no limit -- which is what admission
        does with it -- and is a different answer from a limit of zero.
ScopeQuota.title: ScopeQuota

SecretRotationRequest.description:
Body of the signed-credential rotation route.

Kept materialless for wire compatibility. The route refuses rotation until
protected shared credential distribution and startup recovery exist; an
overlap alone cannot make a process-local key replacement deployment-wide.
SecretRotationRequest.title: SecretRotationRequest

ServerControllerMode.description: Whether this API process actively reconciles workloads and capacity.
ServerControllerMode.title: ServerControllerMode

ServiceDecisionKind.description: What a recorded service decision actually did.
ServiceDecisionKind.title: ServiceDecisionKind

ServiceDecisionRecord.description:
One committed, explained decision about a service.

Append-only per service and bounded per service, so the audit cannot become
the table that fills the disk. The newest row is also the durable cooldown
clock: a decision and the moment it may next be revisited are the same fact,
and keeping them apart is how a cooldown ends up not surviving a restart.
ServiceDecisionRecord.title: ServiceDecisionRecord

ServiceHealthResponse.description:
One managed service's replica health, as an operator can read it.

The three counts are separate fields that must account for every replica
exactly once. A summary that reported only ``healthy`` would make an
unreachable fleet indistinguishable from a dead one at exactly the moment
the difference decides whether accelerators get destroyed.
ServiceHealthResponse.title: ServiceHealthResponse

ServiceObservation.description:
The durable facts one service decision was taken from.

Stored beside the decision rather than recomputed later. A decision explained
by today's state is not explained at all: by the time anyone reads it, the
replicas it counted are gone.
ServiceObservation.title: ServiceObservation

ServiceProbeOutcome.description: What one completed health probe established, including "nothing".
ServiceProbeOutcome.title: ServiceProbeOutcome

ServiceReplicaHealth.description:
What is durably known about one replica, with UNKNOWN as its own answer.

``health`` has three values and the two counters are carried side by side,
so an operator can tell "this replica answered that it is not serving" from
"nobody could reach this replica". Collapsing those into a boolean is the
defect the durable record exists to prevent, and a transport model that
re-collapses them would undo it at the last hop.
ServiceReplicaHealth.title: ServiceReplicaHealth

ServiceReplicaHealthState.description: The health verdict derived from a replica's durable probe counters.
ServiceReplicaHealthState.title: ServiceReplicaHealthState

SessionResponse.description: Authenticated identity and its fully resolved effective authority.
SessionResponse.title: SessionResponse

SubjectUsageRecord.description:
What one person used, and what it cost.

Eyvan settled cost per lease and reported it per pool, so the fleet's
spending was answerable and "who spent it" was not -- a shared project could
see its bill and not its breakdown. Every input already existed: a lease
carries settled cost and accelerator hours, and the workload it belongs to
carries who submitted it.

``unpriced_leases`` is reported rather than folded into zero. A pool with no
declared unit price contributes nothing to ``settled_cost``, and without
this a heavy user of unpriced capacity is indistinguishable from an idle
one -- which is the reading that gets somebody's quota cut.
SubjectUsageRecord.title: SubjectUsageRecord

TeamTier.description:
How much a team-mode account is trusted. Derived, never stored.

``admin`` is whoever holds an active ``fleet_admin`` grant; otherwise
``trusted`` when the account carries ``UserRecord.trusted``; otherwise
``user``. Deriving it keeps the grant table the one source of authority.
TeamTier.title: TeamTier

TpuChipRequest.description:
A share of one TPU host: ``count`` chips, optionally the exact ``indexes``.

Indexes are global within the slice -- host ``index // chips_per_host``,
local chip ``index % chips_per_host`` -- and are kept sorted. Only accepted
by pools that opt into chip sharing; absent, a workload takes its whole cell
exactly as before.
TpuChipRequest.title: TpuChipRequest

TpuQuotaEntry.description:
One zone and accelerator type's quota ceiling, usage, and free balance.

Chips are Cloud TPU quota units, which use the public accelerator suffix:
one ``v6e-8`` slice consumes eight units. ``free_slices`` is that division
already done, because the question an operator actually has is "how many of
these fit", not "how many units are left".
TpuQuotaEntry.title: TpuQuotaEntry

TpuQuotaFailure.description:
One purchase class whose provider read did not succeed.

Reported beside the rows that did succeed rather than collapsing the whole
snapshot: a fleet whose Spot usage is unreadable still has readable
on-demand quota, and hiding one behind the other is how an operator ends up
believing a zone is empty.
TpuQuotaFailure.title: TpuQuotaFailure

TpuQuotaSnapshot.description:
Provider TPU quota, usage, and free balance for one project.

``refreshed_at`` is when the provider was read and ``observed_at`` is when
this response was assembled; ``age_s`` is the distance between them. A
cached snapshot therefore states its own age instead of being presented as
live, which is the difference between "no capacity" and "nobody has looked
recently".
TpuQuotaSnapshot.title: TpuQuotaSnapshot

TpuQuotaState.description:
What one quota row is actually able to say about free capacity.

``USAGE_UNKNOWN`` is the reason this enum exists. Cloud Quotas reports a
limit for a zone whether or not Cloud Monitoring has a matching usage
series, and a row that renders a missing usage as zero claims the entire
quota is free -- the most expensive wrong answer this data can give. The
state is carried on the wire so no renderer has to infer it from a null.
TpuQuotaState.title: TpuQuotaState

TpuQuotaStatus.description: Whether a snapshot describes provider truth, and why not when it does not.
TpuQuotaStatus.title: TpuQuotaStatus

UserProgressReport.description:
One rank's latest self-reported progress.

**Latest per rank, no history.** Upserted on ``(workload_id, attempt, rank)``,
so it is idempotent by overwrite, needs no idempotency key, and cannot grow
without bound. Unbounded user-metric history in the control-plane database is
the thing to refuse now rather than after it has filled a disk.
UserProgressReport.title: UserProgressReport

WarmWindow.description:
A recurring window during which a pool keeps a raised cell floor.

Scale-to-zero saves real money overnight and costs it at 09:00, when every user
pays the full provisioning latency simultaneously. A window is the smallest thing
that fixes that without predicting anything.

Time is a **fixed UTC offset**, not a named zone. Eyvan ships no timezone
database, and a DST-aware window it cannot actually honour would be worse than
one whose limits are stated: a fleet in a DST region shifts by an hour twice a
year, which is visible and adjustable, rather than silently wrong.
WarmWindow.title: WarmWindow

WarmthReport.description: Warm-floor status across every pool, at one moment.
WarmthReport.title: WarmthReport

WebhookCreateRequest.description: Where a project wants its lifecycle events pushed.
WebhookCreateRequest.title: WebhookCreateRequest

WebhookRecord.description:
Where one project wants its lifecycle events pushed.

The audit stream has always been readable, over SSE, by a client willing to
hold a connection open. That is the wrong shape for the things people
actually want notified -- a Slack workspace, a pager, somebody's small
script -- so "tell me when my job finishes" meant writing a poller, and a
poller is how a control plane acquires a hundred clients asking the same
question every five seconds.

The secret is write-only. It is the key the receiver verifies the signature
with; anything that reads a subscription back reads it redacted, because a
signature anybody can forge proves nothing about who sent the request.
WebhookRecord.title: WebhookRecord

WorkerResourceScope.description: Describe whether a workload gang is one worker or one complete atomic cell.
WorkerResourceScope.title: WorkerResourceScope

WorkloadCapacityPhaseProgress.description: Current cells grouped by their durable Eyvan and provider phases.
WorkloadCapacityPhaseProgress.title: WorkloadCapacityPhaseProgress

WorkloadCapacityRequest.description: Exact capacity request after gang-replica and physical-cell expansion.
WorkloadCapacityRequest.title: WorkloadCapacityRequest

WorkloadCapacitySummary.description: Exact-pool capacity counts for a workload's requested physical shape.
WorkloadCapacitySummary.title: WorkloadCapacitySummary

WorkloadDefinition.description: Execution and placement intent accepted by the public API.
WorkloadDefinition.title: WorkloadDefinition

WorkloadDispatchReservation.description:
Durable fence around one possibly-started cell-agent submission.

The reservation is committed before the controller calls the agent and is
compared again when the response is written back.  ``fence`` also binds
secret capabilities to this exact delivery: retrying the same outbox command
replaces it, so capabilities from an abandoned RPC never become live again.
WorkloadDispatchReservation.title: WorkloadDispatchReservation

WorkloadEstimate.description:
Pre-submission cost estimate for one workload definition.

Answers "what will this cost, and will my budget take it" *before* a record
exists -- the question every operator asks and that previously required
submitting and reading the resulting lease's ``reserved_cost``.

Every figure is an estimate over ``estimated_duration_seconds``, which is a
user-supplied number. The estimate is only as honest as that input, and the
field is named to say so rather than presenting a projection as a quote.
WorkloadEstimate.title: WorkloadEstimate

WorkloadEstimateRequest.description: Ask what one workload definition would cost, without submitting it.
WorkloadEstimateRequest.title: WorkloadEstimateRequest

WorkloadExecRequest.description: One diagnostic command to run beside a running workload.
WorkloadExecRequest.title: WorkloadExecRequest

WorkloadExplanation.description:
Why one workload is or is not currently placeable.

Computed on demand by re-running the pure scheduler against current state,
so it always reflects the fleet as it is now rather than a verdict cached
when the workload was last considered. The scheduler already produces the
per-cell detail; persisting it would add a second field to keep in sync at
every ``scheduling_reason`` write site, and would go stale the moment a
cell changed.

``cells`` is bounded for display; ``considered_cell_count`` is the true
number of rejected cells so a truncated list is never mistaken for the
whole fleet.
WorkloadExplanation.title: WorkloadExplanation

WorkloadPoolProgress.description: Stable identity of the exact capacity pool pinned by a workload.
WorkloadPoolProgress.title: WorkloadPoolProgress

WorkloadProgress.description: Read-only autoscaling progress for one submitted workload.
WorkloadProgress.title: WorkloadProgress

WorkloadProgressPhase.description: Operator-facing phase for one workload while capacity is acquired and used.
WorkloadProgressPhase.title: WorkloadProgressPhase

WorkloadSetup.description:
A bash step run on every host of a job, inside the job's own environment.

Exactly one of ``script`` (inline bash) or ``url`` (an ``https://`` script
fetched on the host) is set. ``args`` are passed to the script; ``sha256``,
when given, refuses a fetched script whose bytes differ. The worker runs it
after the job's ``dependencies`` are installed, with ``EYVAN_PYTHON`` naming
the job interpreter, and caches the result by script content and args.
WorkloadSetup.title: WorkloadSetup

WorkloadSpendRecord.description:
What one run used and was charged, with the on-demand alternative.

Computed by the control plane rather than by whoever is asking, because the
honest answer needs pool unit prices and those are a fleet read. Assembling
it in the client meant `eyvan workload cost` listed capacity pools, so the
one command that answers "what did this cost me" was refused to everybody
who could not administer the fleet -- while its own help said nothing about
that.

``priced`` is the field that matters. An unpriced pool settles to zero, so
``settled`` means nothing when this is false, and reporting `$0.00` would
present the absence of a price as the absence of a bill.
WorkloadSpendRecord.title: WorkloadSpendRecord

WorkloadState.description: Durable lifecycle states for a whole workload.
WorkloadState.title: WorkloadState

WorkspaceRef.description:
A packaged working tree to materialize on the host before the workload runs.

Deliberately a property of the *workload*, not of one execution kind. A
workspace answers "what source is on this host", which is independent of
whether the process is launched as a shell command or as a pickled callable.

Modelling it on :class:`CallableExecution` -- where it first appeared,
because callables needed it first -- made that independence untrue in
practice: ``CommandExecution`` has only a command string, so ``eyvan run``
could not ship a working tree at all, and the only way to get your own code
onto an accelerator was to bake an image or use the Python decorator. That
was a modelling accident, not a decision.

The three fields travel together and are validated together: a URI without a
digest cannot be verified, and a signature without a URI signs nothing.
WorkspaceRef.title: WorkspaceRef

post.description:
Close an elapsed budget period without waiting for the next settlement.

Not a force-reset: a period that has not elapsed is left alone, because
zeroing it would erase spend the limit is still meant to bind. Idempotent
-- rolling twice in one period is the second call returning the record
unchanged.

get.description:
Report a budget's period window and its projected end-of-period spend.

The forecast assumes every active lease runs to the end of the window --
the pessimistic reading, deliberately, because this number exists to warn
before a hard limit starts refusing admission.

Report the code this plane is running, not only its version string.

Every component of this system ships one version, so an operator cannot
use it to answer the question an upgrade actually raises: is the plane
this proof polled the build the receipt claims? A hardware proof has
already been run against a stale agent and read as evidence.

Authenticated, because a build digest and an interpreter version are a
fingerprint. It costs one cached tree walk per process.
List enabled pools available to a workload scope, optionally filtered by TPU shape.

schema.title: Response List Capacity Pools Api V1 Capacity Pools Get

get.description: Show one capacity pool record.

Report accrued and idle cell cost across the fleet or one pool.

The idle figure is not derivable from budgets: an idle cell holds no lease,
so nothing settles and nothing is charged to a project. This is the only
place a fleet's unused-but-paid-for capacity is visible.
Report which build every reachable cell agent runs, beside this plane's.

Report grid intensity for the regions this fleet occupies.

Every entry carries ``no_provider`` unless an operator has configured a
source, and none ships. That is the answer, not a gap in it: a carbon
feature whose unconfigured state is an empty response cannot be told
apart from a broken one, and one whose unconfigured state is *zero*
claims every grid is clean.

Reporting only. Nothing in the placement path consults this, and a test
asserts the scheduler and the planner do not import the module behind
it -- a number nobody has validated would otherwise steer scheduling
while looking deliberate.

Report how long each pool takes to hand over usable capacity.

The same ``provision_latencies_s`` the scheduler ranks pools on, which is
why every figure carries its sample count: a p95 over three provisions is
not a p95, and presenting one as equivalent to a p95 over three hundred
invites the confident wrong decision this exists to prevent.
List cells an agent still holds that no control-plane record claims.

Report submitted-vs-admitted counts over recent time buckets.

Derived from the audit ledger, which already records both with timestamps
and a monotonic sequence -- so this is a query over data that exists rather
than a second time-series store to prune, back up, and keep consistent.

Report provider TPU quota, live usage, and free balance per zone and type.

The numbers ``eyvan autoscale generate`` already reads, answered for the
operator choosing where to run instead of only for the generator. Two
provider reads back it -- Spot and on-demand are separate quota metrics --
and either may fail on its own, so a failed class is reported beside the
rows that succeeded rather than collapsing the whole snapshot.

A zone whose Cloud Monitoring usage series is missing is reported as
``usage_unknown`` with no free balance at all. It is never reported as
zero usage, because a quota limit presented as free capacity is the one
answer here that costs money to act on.

Read-only and cached for ``TPU_QUOTA_CACHE_TTL_S``: every response states
when the provider was actually read, so a cached number is never
presented as a live one. Authorized exactly as the pool listing it reads
its provider projects from.

Report each pool's warm floor and whether it is currently held.

Pair this with ``/capacity/billing``: warm capacity is deliberately idle,
so its cost must be subtracted from the fleet's idle cost before that
number means anything. Without the pairing, the only safe reaction to an
unexplained idle figure is to delete the warm floor -- undoing the fix.

schema.title: Response List Cells Api V1 Cells Get

post.description:
Submit a small pipeline of dependent workloads in one transaction.

Each node is an ordinary durable workload. A node with predecessors is
created unschedulable and released once every predecessor has succeeded; if
one fails or is cancelled, its dependents are cancelled rather than left
waiting forever. Dependencies order execution only -- results travel as
``eyvan://`` result URIs, not through the control plane.

get.description:
Serve the browser's identity configuration at runtime.

The dashboard's OIDC issuer and client id were compiled into the bundle
by ``VITE_`` build arguments, so one image could serve exactly one
identity provider -- and an operator with two environments had to build
two images that differed in nothing else.

Unauthenticated on purpose, and safe: an issuer URL and a public OAuth
client id are both things the browser is about to send to the identity
provider in a redirect anyway. Nothing here is a secret, and requiring a
token to learn how to obtain a token is a loop.

Null when unconfigured rather than absent, so a caller can tell "this
control plane runs without OIDC" from "this control plane is too old to
answer".

``development_auth`` names the third state, which the browser could not
previously see. A plane with no OIDC is not necessarily misconfigured:
the loopback development plane every laptop runs has none by design, and
the dashboard used to greet it by naming two build-time ``VITE_``
variables of a bundle the reader never built. Reported as the mode's own
name so the page can say what is true of *this* plane rather than
recite the general case.

The home plane refuses to issue past its own limit, counting both what it
has already granted away and what it has itself spent. That one check is
the entire cross-plane guarantee -- no plane consults another at
admission time, because the slices were bounded when they were cut.

delete.description:
Withdraw a peer's authority to spend.

Returns the grant rather than 204: revocation stops *new* admission and
says nothing about what already ran, and ``reported_spend`` on the
returned record is what that distinction looks like in numbers.

Stops new admission and does not disturb what is already running: a quota

Submit differently-shaped workloads that must admit together.

Every member is created unschedulable and all are released in one
transaction once each is independently placeable in the same pass. This is
a feasibility gate, not a reservation: capacity can still be taken between
that answer and the members' leases. What it prevents is half a group
holding accelerators while the rest is structurally infeasible.

get.description:
Liveness: this process is running and its event loop answers.

Deliberately does **not** touch the database, even though a probe that
did would look more thorough. Liveness failure means *restart me*, and a
liveness probe that depends on a shared database restarts every replica
at once the moment that database blips -- turning a recoverable outage
into a total one, then preventing recovery by stampeding reconnections.

Whether this replica can usefully serve is a different question with a
different consequence, and it is answered by ``/readyz``.

``already_tracing`` is the half that decides whether the numbers mean

so a snapshot from a tracker this call had to switch on covers

get.description:

The one answer that identifies a wedged scheduler. Every external signal
looks identical when the leader holds its lease and advances nothing --
the API answers, health is green -- and the difference is which frame the
process is sitting in.

Taken as a snapshot rather than by suspending the process: a consistent
dump bought with a stop-the-world pause would be an outage taken to
investigate a stall.

post.description:
Answer one read-only statement against this plane's own database.

The triage surface the typed endpoints cannot cover: during an incident
the question is usually a join nobody anticipated, and the alternative to
this is an operator opening ``psql`` on the head with write access and no
ledger entry.

Read-ness is enforced by the transaction rather than by inspecting the
SQL, and the authorization is ``MANAGE_FLEET`` because the scope of a raw
read is the whole database rather than the caller's grants.

post.description:
Refuse unsupported deployment-wide signing credential rotation.

No protected shared credential-version store or startup hydration exists
yet. Installing random material in this process would strand dispatches
on other replicas and resurrect retired keys on restart. A ledger commit
cannot repair that, and an uncertain commit must not leave a signer live.
Keep the authorized route discoverable, but change neither key nor ledger.

get.description:
Return the caller's effective authority after all grants are resolved.

The dependency has already verified the request credential and unioned
its claim grants with unexpired durable grants. The dashboard consumes
this response rather than decoding an unverified JWT payload and
pretending that payload includes the server's durable authority.

Registered projects are returned only when this principal has at least
one permission there. ``org_id``/``project_id`` may name a preferred
legacy scope that predates the tenant registry; it is included only if
the same authorizer that guards API operations says it is effective.

Report which durability invariants the fleet is currently violating.

The point-in-time half only. Budget monotonicity and storage growth are
statements about a *sequence* of observations, so a single request
cannot settle them and this does not pretend to -- a soak run holds the
previous snapshot and compares.

An empty ``violations`` list is a real claim, not a default: every check
has a test that makes it fire, so silence here means the checks ran and
found nothing rather than that nothing ran.

schema.title: Response Fleet Invariants Api V1 System Invariants Get

post.description: Return invariant state plus coverage for one exact frozen proof manifest.

schema.title: Response Proof Scoped Fleet Invariants Api V1 System Invariants Soak Post
Response Reconcile Once Api V1 System Reconcile Post

post.description:
Accept one externally measured, proof-bound P8 sample.

The control plane cannot be the source of its own resource evidence: a
process reporting its own RSS proves nothing about a process that is
leaking, and no amount of durable state tells it what a provider still
bills for. So this route only *stores* what a separate monitor measured
and posted, and :func:`proof_scoped_fleet_invariants` republishes it
unchanged. Nothing here infers, defaults, or completes a sample.

The body is bounded while it is read rather than after it is buffered,
the eight closed keys must be exactly right, and every value must
already have the type it will be republished with -- numeric text is
refused rather than coerced, because a stored ``12`` and a posted
``"12"`` would be two different pieces of evidence.

Only the most recent sample is kept, and only in this process. It is a
measurement, not fleet state: a replica that restarts has not lost a
record, it has stopped having a current one, and reporting no evidence
until the monitor posts again is the truthful answer.

The fleet's spending was answerable per pool and never per person, so a

Read permission, not project administration. The people sharing a

schema.title: Response List Webhooks Api V1 Webhooks Get

post.description:
Register where this project's lifecycle events should be pushed.

The response is the only time the signing key is visible, and it is the
one the caller supplied: reads redact it, because a signature anybody
can forge proves nothing about who sent a delivery.

delete.description: Stop delivering to one subscription and forget it.

schema.title: Response List Workloads Api V1 Workloads Get

post.description:
Estimate what a workload would cost, before any record exists.

Not a scheduling dry run: it consults declared pool attributes and prices,
never live cell availability, because an estimate that claimed to predict
placement would be wrong the moment the fleet moved. No ``Idempotency-Key``
-- it writes nothing.

Cancel one workload, and by default every descendant under it.

``cascade=false`` cancels exactly this workload. That is the escape hatch
for a stored tree deeper than the traversal limit: without it such a
parent could never be cancelled at all, because every attempt failed on
the walk before reaching the workload the caller actually named.

get.description: Return the direct children of one workload in a job tree.

schema.title: Response List Child Workloads Api V1 Workloads  Workload Id  Children Get

get.description:
Return what one run used and was charged, with the alternative.

Authorized as a read of the workload it is about. The client used to
assemble this itself, which meant listing capacity pools for their unit
prices -- a fleet read -- so the one command that answers "what did this
cost me" was refused to everybody who could not administer the fleet.
List the replicas of a service that are currently able to serve.

post.description:
Run one diagnostic command beside every rank of a running workload.

``OPERATE`` rather than ``READ``: this starts a process on a host that
is running someone's job. It is not a mutation of the workload, but it
is not an observation either, and treating it as one would let a viewer
run commands on the fleet.

get.description:
Return why one workload is or is not currently placeable.

Recomputed on demand from the pure scheduler, so it reflects the fleet
as it is now rather than the verdict from the last scheduling pass.

post.description:
Settle a workload whose stop the worker will never confirm.

Break glass. It gives up the cell rather than returning it, because the
process may still be running on a host nobody could stop.

Interrupt one attempt and let it reschedule on its preemption budget.

The move an operator wants when an attempt is wedged on a bad host but
the job itself is fine: stop this attempt, put the workload back in the
queue, and let placement pick somewhere else. Cancelling would end the
job, and waiting for a timeout wastes the accelerator until it fires.

Charged to the *preemption* budget rather than the failure budget. A
capacity loss is charged against ``max_retries``, which a spot job sets
to 0 precisely because it expects to be interrupted -- so charging a kick
there would kill the job an operator was trying to move. The audit action
stays distinct from a provider reclamation, because who interrupted the
attempt is exactly what a later reader needs.

get.description:
Return one resumable page of structured logs, merged across ranks.

Separate from ``/logs`` rather than a format parameter on it: that route
is declared ``PlainTextResponse`` and every consumer reads it as bytes.

``after`` is the ``next_cursor`` from a previous page, which carries the
attempt it came from. A cursor from a superseded attempt is reported as
``attempt_changed`` and the read restarts, because the alternative --
continuing quietly -- shows the new attempt's first lines appended to the
old attempt's tail and reads as a job that resumed.

Follow one workload's structured logs as they are produced.

A distinct route rather than a reuse of ``/events/stream``: that stream
is scoped to (org, project) and keyed on the audit table's BIGSERIAL,
while log records are per-(workload, attempt, rank) and have no global
sequence at all. They share this module's transport and nothing else.

``Last-Event-ID`` is the same ``"{attempt}:{rank}=cursor|..."`` the
paged route returns, so a browser reconnecting resumes every rank where
it left off rather than replaying from the tail.

``include_status=true`` opts into bounded ``log.page_status`` events,
including on empty pages, distinguishing unavailable, suppressed or
incomplete output from healthy silence. Unchanged status is not repeated.
The default retains the legacy record-only wire format during rollout.

Authorization happens here, before the generator exists. A check inside
it would run after the response was committed, and the caller would see
``200`` followed by silence -- indistinguishable from a quiet job.

Return live process detail for one workload attempt.

Reading process state is an observation, not a mutation, so it needs
only the READ that ``get_workload`` already enforces for this scope.
Return autoscaler and provider lifecycle progress for one workload.

List what was observed, what was decided, and why -- newest first.

The decision carries the observation it was taken from rather than a
pointer to state that has since moved on, so an operator reading it
tomorrow reconstructs the call instead of guessing at it.

schema.title: Response List Service Decisions Api V1 Workloads  Workload Id  Service Decisions Get

get.description:
Report each replica's durable health, with UNKNOWN kept distinct.

Read-only, and it never converts an absence into a verdict: a service
that declares no health path comes back ``probing_enabled=false`` with
every replica ``unknown`` and ``probed=false``, which says nothing was
asked -- not that anything failed.

Liveness: this process is running and its event loop answers.

Deliberately does **not** touch the database, even though a probe that
did would look more thorough. Liveness failure means *restart me*, and a
liveness probe that depends on a shared database restarts every replica
at once the moment that database blips -- turning a recoverable outage
into a total one, then preventing recovery by stampeding reconnections.

Whether this replica can usefully serve is a different question with a
different consequence, and it is answered by ``/readyz``.
